**A tensor's shape is not its physical storage order.** Strides specify how far to move in storage when advancing along each dimension. Transposing a matrix usually changes those strides without rearranging its underlying elements. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)

For a contiguous 2-by-3 matrix, transposition yields a 3-by-2 view whose logical row order no longer matches a simple contiguous traversal. Flattening that transposed layout as a no-copy view may be impossible with the requested strides.

`view()` requires the requested shape to be compatible with existing storage and strides. `reshape()` uses a view when possible and otherwise may copy. Calling `contiguous()` explicitly requests an appropriate contiguous copy when one is needed.

**Do not assume every reshape aliases or every noncontiguous tensor forbids every view.** Some reshapes remain compatible, and others allocate. Check shape, stride, and aliasing when debugging in-place changes or performance. A costly layout copy can dominate a small operation, while a mistaken axis interpretation can silently compute the wrong result even when all dimensions are legal.

**Technical details and references.**

`view()` reinterprets shape without copying only when strides are compatible. `reshape()` returns a view when possible and otherwise may allocate a copy. Transpose/permute usually changes strides rather than rearranging storage, producing a noncontiguous view. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/index.html)

A tensor can be noncontiguous yet still permit some views, so “view requires contiguous” is an oversimplification. Use `contiguous()` when an explicit layout copy is appropriate, but account for its cost. Never rely on `reshape()` always aliasing or always copying. Check strides, shape, and mutation semantics when debugging a silently incorrect axis manipulation.
